source.pageTitle: Brazil: Electoral court fines Meta $1.3M for noncompliance

evidence.sourceExcerpt: Brazil: Electoral court fines Meta $1.3M for noncompliance Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites In focus COP31 Ukraine war Nvidia Latest audio Latest videos Live TV Advertisement https://p.dw.com/p/5PL2q Prefer DW on Google The fine was based on Meta's overall handling of the court orders Image: Thibault Camus/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement Brazil's top electoral court has ordered Meta to pay 7.5 million reais ($1.34 million; €1.22 million) for failing to fully comply with judicial orders during last month's presidential election. However, the judicial body has so far found no evidence that Meta deliberately acted to influence the election outcome. Ahead of the runoff vote on October 25, leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's coalition filed a complaint, accusing Meta of "algorithmic manipulation" favoring his far-right rival Flavio Bolsonaro. Platforms owned by Meta include Facebook , Instagram and WhatsApp. Meta told the court last month that it had implemented measures to guarantee equal treatment for both campaigns. Meta lacked transparency, court says The Superior Electoral Court (TSE) unanimously ruled on Tuesday to impose the 7.5 million reais fine on the US tech giant. Meta missed deadlines and lacked transparency in its investigation, the court said. On the other hand, the court's reporting judge Marco Aurelio Belizze wrote in his ruling that there were no preliminary evidence indicating that any intentional actions were taken to influence the election. "That ​conclusion would require robust evidence, to be produced through the appropriate legal proceedings," he said. In his victory speech, Lula reiterated that Brazil would 'not accept being anyone’s backyard,' a recurring campaign message defending the country’s sovereignty against US influence Image: Natacha Pisarenko/AP Photo/picture alliance According to Bellizze, the fine was based on Meta's overall handling of the court orders, including delays, incomplete disclosures, and challenges in verifying some of the information it provided. In a statement on Wednesday, Meta strongly denied the court's ruling. "We will continue to present the facts and defend ourselves against false allegations in the ‌ongoing ​legal proceedings," Meta said in a statement on Wednesday. Lula vows to rein in social media Lula defeated Bolsonaro in a tight run-off in October 25 with him winning 51.7% of the vote against Bolsonaro's 48.2%. In his victory speech, Lula urged more regulation of big tech platforms after allegations that Meta interfered in the race. "We had to overcome foreign interference in the election, coming from outside through digital platforms that we will have to regulate," he said. It's a remarkable political comeback for Lula who trailed in the first round. source.pageTitle: Security Flaws Across UK Government Sites Exposed ‘God-Tier’ Information | WIRED

evidence.sourceExcerpt: Security Flaws Across UK Government Sites Exposed ‘God-Tier’ Information | WIRED Skip to main content Save this story Save this story A security researcher has found more than 100 serious vulnerabilities in publicly available UK government code, putting sensitive data at risk as a result of poor cyber hygiene. The UK government has defaulted to openly publishing code it produces with public money for around a decade because it’s transparent, and making it easier for code to be reused is cost-efficient. This includes within the Department of Health and Social Care, and the Home Office, as well as local authorities. But funding squeezes have left departments neglecting maintenance and improvement of their technology estate. While ControlPlane security researcher Chris Nesbitt-Smith found the vulnerabilities using Claude’s Opus and Sonnet AI models, he says that he used consumer-grade models on a laptop and that many of the issues could have been caught by a routine IT health check. “None of this is the level of sophistication that general media is worried about in terms of cyber attacks,” he tells WIRED. “It’s all daft stuff.” In the most serious case he identified, the Planning Inspectorate, which handles land-use matters across England, had failed to fully remove a login after it accidentally committed them to public repository GitHub . The fact the credentials gave such wide access—and seemingly didn’t expire—compounded with the agency’s accidental publication of them, “made it particularly dangerous for them.” The complete Microsoft Entra ID would have given “god-tier” read and write access to all SharePoint sites and private employee OneDrive accounts, according to Nesbitt-Smith, including HR records. It also would have given access to sensitive libraries which safeguard evidence under legal hold for statutory planning inquiries and appeals, according to the security researcher who found it. “The option for ransomwaring them, for encrypting all the data, or just stealing all the data, was abundantly there,” Nesbitt-Smith says. A spokesperson for the Planning Inspectorate told WIRED its cyber monitoring tools immediately detected Nesbitt-Smith’s activity in August and that it had already been handling this as a cyber incident when ControlPlane made contact. The agency identified and fixed this vulnerability within 20 minutes of the report and verified that no data breach occurred. “We have reviewed and strengthened our systems and processes to prevent this type of issue recurring and we are grateful for the researcher’s work and for alerting us to it,” they told WIRED. The Planning Inspectorate issue “isn’t about open source but internal housekeeping when using public tools,” Amanda Brock, chief executive officer of nonprofit industry group OpenUK. “That data was exposed because of a failure not to follow good process,” she adds. “That’s not an open source security issue.” In around two-thirds of the 349 public sector codebases across 33 organizations Nesbitt-Smith scanned, he said he found vulnerabilities. Several of these were found in the Department of Education’s code, including in a procurement service used by schools, in a teacher application service containing personal details, qualifications, employment history and identity documents, and England’s main register of government-funded training providers and apprenticeships. He also found a vulnerability in a Scottish Government open data portal which would have allowed any visitor to read administrative account information and to change site configuration. The organizations have since dealt with the issues. Recently, there have been arguments for public sector departments to stop publishing source code in the open, now that AI has accelerated vulnerability discovery. The NHS reportedly ordered technology teams to transition away from open source code in May amid security concerns about the impact of AI models. Doing this without immediately fixing the underlying issues
